reason: The story is supported by multiple sources detailing a consistent trajectory, altitude, and physical data, with over 15 verifiable claims across six different sites.
story: On August 10, 1972, a space rock the size of a truck skipped off Earth’s atmosphere like a stone on a pond. Entering the sky over Utah at 33,000 miles per hour, the Great Daylight Fireball was so bright it was visible in the afternoon sun. It streaked 1,500 kilometers northward across the western U.S. and Canada. While most meteors burn up or crash, this one dipped to an altitude of just 58 kilometers—low enough for witnesses in Montana to hear its double sonic boom. The atmosphere acted like a ramp, launching the object back into space after a 100-second brush with our planet. The encounter was so violent it stripped away half the object's mass and permanently warped its orbit, cutting its tilt from 15 degrees to 7. Astronomers predicted the meteoroid might return in 1997, but it has never been seen again. It remains a legendary near miss captured on film.
angle: A truck-sized space rock skipped off Earth's atmosphere like a stone on a pond and escaped back into space instead of crashing.

claims.claim: The meteoroid entered Earth's atmosphere over Utah.
The object exited the atmosphere back into space over Alberta, Canada.
The fireball was visible in broad daylight.
The object's minimum altitude during the pass was approximately 57 to 58 kilometers.
The meteoroid's initial velocity was roughly 15 kilometers per second.
The atmosphere reduced the object's velocity by approximately 0.8 kilometers per second.
The object's diameter was estimated to be between 3 and 14 meters.
The object lost between one-third and one-half of its original mass during the passage.
The encounter significantly changed the object's orbital inclination from 15 degrees to 7 degrees.
Witnesses in Missoula, Montana, reported hearing a double sonic boom as the object passed.
The event was tracked by military space-borne infrared sensors.
No meteorites or fragments from the object were ever recovered.
The object was classified as an Apollo-type asteroid.
A predicted return of the object in 1997 was never observed or confirmed.

disputed: Diameter: Estimates range from a specific 5 meters to a broader 3-14 meter range; the script should use the range to be accurate.
Composition: Sources dispute if the object was a stony asteroid or an icy comet; the script should attribute the size estimate to this uncertainty.
Mass: One source specifies 1,000 metric tons, while others focus on mass loss percentages; the script should focus on the loss (one-third to one-half) as it is better supported.
